sections.heading: Wondering at what you have done
sections.text: Lord Jesus, I can hardly take in that you became one of us, went to the cross, truly died, and were laid in a grave. And yet the grave is empty. You are alive. The Gospels bear witness to it, your first followers saw you, and your Spirit has made the truth of it real to me. Help me not to treat this as a distant fact, but as the center of my life and worship.
theological_themes: The incarnation, death, burial, and bodily resurrection of Christ are the foundation of Christian faith and worship.
The resurrection is publicly witnessed in Scripture and personally received by faith through the Spirit’s work.

scripture_references.connection: Paul summarizes the gospel as Christ’s death, burial, resurrection, and appearances to witnesses. This grounds the prayer’s wonder not in private feeling alone, but in the apostolic testimony to historical events.
The empty tomb and angelic announcement show that Jesus was not held by death. This supports the prayer’s movement from the grave to adoring confidence that Christ is risen.

sections.heading: Sharing your death so I can live differently
sections.text: Unite me more deeply to you, so that what is dead in me can stay dead. I want to be buried with you in relation to sin, selfishness, and the pull of this world. Do not let me keep listening to the old voices that flatter and tempt me. Deliver me from desires that promise life but lead me away from you.
theological_themes: Believers are united to Christ in his death and resurrection, so the old life is to be counted dead and the new life lived to God.
Sin is not merely bad behavior but a power that deceives and must be decisively rejected.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that those united to Christ share in his death and resurrection, and therefore must consider themselves dead to sin and alive to God. This directly undergirds the prayer’s request to die with Christ and rise into new life.
John contrasts love for the world’s desires with doing the will of God. This helps frame the prayer’s longing to be freed from the world’s seductive pull.

sections.heading: Putting to death what still clings to me
sections.text: Lord, there is still so much wrong in me. Put it to death. There is still so much of my old self at work in me. Do not let me make peace with it. Cleanse me from selfishness, from being controlled by what people think, from craving approval, from being embarrassed to belong to you, and from wanting to look impressive, educated, relevant, or acceptable more than I want to be faithful. Teach me to treat my old life as crucified, not as something to feed and protect.
theological_themes: Sanctification includes active repentance and mortification: putting sinful desires to death by the power of God.
The desire for human approval can become a form of bondage that competes with faithfulness to Christ.

scripture_references.connection: Paul commands believers to put to death what belongs to the earthly nature and to put on the new self. This supports the prayer’s concrete request for God to kill selfishness and old patterns rather than merely restrain them.
Paul contrasts seeking human approval with being a servant of Christ. This fits the prayer’s concern about fear of people, craving approval, and shaping oneself to be acceptable rather than faithful.

sections.heading: Standing with you when obedience costs me
sections.text: Keep me close to my crucified Savior. Make me willing to be misunderstood, rejected, or thought out of step if obedience to you requires it. Give me courage to receive and hold fast to truths people may dislike or dismiss, as long as they are truly yours. Do not let me drift away from the path of your will. Make me steady, resolved, and satisfied in Christ.
theological_themes: Following Christ includes taking up the cross and accepting rejection for his sake.
Faithfulness requires holding to God’s truth with humility and courage, even when it is unpopular.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus calls his disciples to deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow him without being ashamed of him. This grounds the prayer’s willingness to stand with the rejected Savior.
Paul urges Timothy not to be ashamed of testimony about Christ, but to guard the good deposit entrusted to him. This supports the prayer’s request for courage to hold fast to truth under pressure.

sections.heading: Living in the power of your resurrection
sections.text: Strengthen me for the battles ahead. Give me courage for every trial, and give me grace for every joy, so that hardship does not crush me and comfort does not corrupt me. Make me holy and genuinely glad in you. Free me from every desire that is out of step with your heart. Let more and more of your resurrection life govern me, shape my choices, and strengthen me from the inside out.
theological_themes: The risen Christ gives power for perseverance, holiness, joy, and obedience.
Both suffering and blessing require grace: trials can discourage faith, and joys can become idols if not received before God.

scripture_references.connection: Paul longs to know Christ, the power of his resurrection, and fellowship in his sufferings while pressing on toward the goal. This supports the prayer’s desire for resurrection life that reshapes endurance and holiness.
Paul prays that believers would know the immeasurable power of God at work in them, the same power displayed in raising Christ. This illuminates the prayer’s request to walk in resurrection strength.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s phrase about being thought “old-fashioned” and the desire to be “cultivated or modern” reflects a particular cultural pressure: wanting social respectability or intellectual fashion more than faithfulness. I preserved the concern without implying that education, culture, or contemporary expression are inherently wrong.

The prayer’s language of being crucified with Christ and putting sin to death can be intense. I kept the biblical force of mortification while avoiding any implication of self-harm; the meaning is spiritual repentance and Spirit-empowered rejection of sin.
significant_interpretive_choices: I rendered “the voice of the charmer” as old voices that flatter and tempt, taking it as the seductive power of sin, the world, and the devil rather than a specific reference to one temptation.

I treated “my heart’s experience knows it” as the Spirit making the truth of Christ’s resurrection real to the believer, while keeping the primary basis of confidence in Scripture and apostolic witness.
I rendered “Christ-contained” as being satisfied in Christ, since the original appears to mean inwardly held, steadied, and sufficient in Christ rather than self-contained independence.
